newsitem.title: GERMANY: CDU breathes sigh of relief after Hesse vote.
newsitem.headline: CDU breathes sigh of relief after Hesse vote.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) said on Monday they got an encouraging boost from the weekend Hesse elections but commentators warned the outcome showed voter dissatisfaction with Germany's mainstream parties.
The CDU, under fire in Bonn for failing to stop unemployment reaching 1930s levels, increased its vote by one percentage point to 33.0 percent.
But in what all parties attributed to general discontent with politics, voter turnout in warm and sunny weather dropped to 66.0 percent from 71.3 in 1993.
CDU officials quickly seized on the outcome, saying the results endorsed Kohl's drive for tax and pension reforms.

Newspapers said the CDU was wrong to draw such a conclusion from a result which contrasts with recent national opinion polls showing his ruling coalition would lose its majority if a general election were held now.

The vote in Hesse, one of Germany's wealthiest states with 4.5 million eligible voters, was dominated by local issues but carried national implications as one of only two elections this year. Hamburg votes in September.

"Hesse was no foretaste of the general election, but next to Hamburg the only test run for Bonn this year. And the mood has rarely been this bad," wrote the Handelsblatt business daily in a commentary.
The Social Democrats, the main opposition party in Bonn, also posted modest gains in Hesse, gaining 1.6 points to 38.0 percent compared with the last local election in 1993.

"They may only have been local elections," wrote Die Welt. "But they reflect national developments. The coalition is in critical condition with the high unemployment, financial difficulties and tax reform debate."
The main losers in Hesse were the smaller parties. The environmentalist Greens stagnated while the liberal Free Democrats (FDP) and far-right Republicans suffered losses.
The Greens were unchanged at 11.0 percent, the FDP dropped to 4.0 percent from 5.1 percent and the Republicans declined to 6.6 percent from 8.3 percent.
In Germany's financial capital Frankfurt, a city of 660,000 people, the CDU recorded impressive gains owing mainly to the popularity of mayor Petra Roth.

"This result, coming a year and a half before the general elections, should help Chancellor Kohl," she said. "It shows that he can rely on Frankfurt. I'm proud that in Frankfurt the CDU was elected as a modern, big-city party."
The SPD, its image dented by years of infighting with the Greens, saw its vote fall to 29.1 percent from 32.0 percent, its worst result in Frankfurt since the war.

The Greens gained 2.9 points to 16.9 percent and the FDP, helped by their leading candidate. Ignatz Bubis, Germany's Jewish leader, entered the city's parliament for the first time in 16 years with 5.6 percent.
